utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to move the ELMO either forward or back so that it's not in the way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, last week just before the break, we were talking about the one night or the one evening when you stayed late at the KP Dom, and you said it was to get the bakery started. You remember that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we were talking about that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And when you testified to this event in your direct examination, you said that it was in late May of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is right. It is most probably right, late May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you gave an interview to the investigators of the Prosecutor's office on the first day, that is the 5th of June, 2000, you told them that night or that evening when you stayed late was most probably around the end of June, beginning of July. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember saying that. However, since that certainly happened earlier, because there was no electricity in May, this was probably an error in dates, because this certainly happened much earlier, before the tragedy in my family took place. So that's why it was probably the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But, sir, you knew about that connection with the time even in June of last year when you talked to the investigators, and yet you said it was in June, possibly July. You've changed the date, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not change it on purpose, for sure, but it is possible that I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You talked about how the -- you stayed until 9.00, because that's when the bakers were baking the bread. Isn't it true that the bakers, when they came, came much later? According to the city baker himself, they came at 3.00 in the morning whenever they had to bake bread, not 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, first of all, the bakery had to be started up. Then if I'm not mistaken, at least 12 hours were required for the bakery to get going, because it uses solid fuel, wood. Then it is only after 12 hours that the bakery could be used; that is to say, that is when bread could actually be baked, because that is the furnace that requires more time to attain a certain temperature in order to make it possible for bread to be baked. As soon as Relja said that he didn't need any material from the central warehouse, because you may recall that I said because of those keys I stayed back anyway, he stayed on to finish some minor details and also to get the fire started in the furnace in the bakery. I hope you will understand what I'm saying. This is a furnace that is fired by solid fuel, firewood, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you often met with Muslim detainees upon their request; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that that was often. If I met a few people, with a person perhaps once, with somebody else perhaps two or three times, I wouldn't call that often. Because when I say "often," I would imply doing something several times during the course of one day, so I wouldn't call it often. I don't know how people understand this word "often."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: According to your words in your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor last year, you said, "I would habitually meet with more prominent people in town who were detained at the KP Dom."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for me, prominent people are doctors, teachers, and any well-intentioned person, any person of goodwill and good intentions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: My emphasis was on the word "habitually." You met perhaps not often but habitually; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what happened, happened. Perhaps I used that word "habitually," because these people who were detained, it depended on whether they were allowed all these things by the guards and by the guard on duty at the entrance desk, whether they would allow them whatever. So whoever was allowed by the guard on duty to come, and if he asked me whether I would see him, I did not refuse to see anyone, regardless of who asked to see me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So the procedure for a detainee to see you was that the request would be made through the guards, and then the guards would ask you if you would meet with them; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the guard would come and tell me, "Milorad, can you see such-and-such a person?" I would say yes, and then he would bring that person who he had mentioned to me and then I would briefly talk to that person. If there was coffee, then we would have a coffee and a cigarette. These were not long conversations. It would be about as long as it takes to smoke a cigarette, and you can smoke a cigarette in, say, five to ten minutes, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: These were not strictly social calls, were they? When people asked to see you, it wasn't always in your personal capacity as a friend or an acquaintance; often they asked to see you -- or most of the time they asked to see you because you were the warden. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, though, that it wasn't all because of that, although there is some of that as well. They wanted to come and see me primarily so that some of them who were coming for the first time would ask me whether I knew what their situation was, and it also happened that they would ask for toiletries that they needed, if there weren't any. And it wasn't any special kind of socialising or long conversations. It's not because they knew I was warden, because every one of them who came to see me, I assert to you here from this stand, that I told them all the truth, that I was warden in charge of the economic part. They knew that this was rented out to the military and they knew that it was the military that was in charge of them, the military command. I did not conceal that from them, never, not from a single one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So the people, the detainees who came to see you, came to ask you for help; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually help. As I told you, those who would come for the first time would ask me whether I knew what their fate was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Among the people whom you met with were [redacted] [redacted], Husein Lojo, Safet Avdic, RJ, and Dr. Avdo Softalija; right? These were some of the prominent members of the community whom you met with.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, I do not remember that all these people came to see me. I don't remember that Mr. Safet Avdic came to see me, and I don't remember this other doctor that you mentioned. Softalija did you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The chief of the medical centre in Foca, the person that we discussed earlier. Sadinlija. I'm sorry. I mispronounced it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sadinlija. Dr. Sadinlija. Oh, Dr. Sadinlija, yes. He was at the health centre. He was not at the hospital. During those first days, he came to see me at the office. I think it was the end of April, or rather, in the month of April. The first conversation I had was precisely with Mr. Sadinlija. He asked to speak with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You also met with [redacted], who was a prominent Muslim politician; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that encounter. I personally think that I did not meet with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You also met with three members of the Cengic family, right, before their release? They were related to the assembly deputy Muhamed Cengic, from Miljevina.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, it seems to me that we discussed that. That meeting was when the commander of the Tactical Group came, and when he said that he would like to have a meeting in my office with three men, three men who were supposed to be released. I think that we discussed that and I explained that. However, if necessary, I can explain this same situation once again as to how this happened and that they were taken to Belgrade, in the words of the commander. Whether they were actually taken or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The Commander of the Tactical Group, Marko Kovac, came to you and asked if he could finish a job here and if you could have those three detainees brought to him; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't do that. He said to me, "Milorad, can I have a meeting with three detained persons who are supposed to be released and sent to Belgrade?" In the meantime, these three persons had already come to my office, and a moment before that, I had ordered coffee. And then when they had their meeting, their conversation, I left. I really don't know what they discussed, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, on the 6th of June, 2000, during your interview with investigators of the Prosecutor's office, you gave the following description of that meeting, and I'm reading from the English, page 31: "One morning, the commander of the Tactical Group came to my office, greeted me, and asked me, `Milorad, can I do something here, finish a job here?' I said, `Yes, you can. What is it about?' He said,`I would need Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. three detainees to come here.' Of course I approved it, and these three detainees were brought to my office later." That's how you described that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any difference. The meaning of what I said then and now is the same, although I perhaps have not used the same words. It's logical that I cannot remember it all word for word, but I think that the meaning is the same, and my answer is, therefore, the same now as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The Commander of the Tactical Group, Marko Kovac, came to you to ask you if he could finish a job there and you said yes; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What else could I have said? I said yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And when he asked specifically for three Muslim detainees to be brought to your office, you approved it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, he did not ask for that from my office. I assume - this is the most probable option - he told somebody before hand, either the guard on duty or some other person, that these men should be brought there. It was not that he said from my office where they should be brought, or he didn't inform anyone from my office. That means that he had agreed with someone, as he was entering the building of the KP Dom, probably the duty officer or someone else - I don't know to whom - but people -- these men were brought to him to my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: These men were brought to your office only because you approved it, not because anybody made any arrangements beforehand; right? According to your own description, that was the way things happened.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my personal opinion, when I say that he had agreed upon something beforehand, that meant that he agreed with the guard on duty where these people should be brought to him, and they were brought to see him in that office, and I did not refuse him. I did not say that he could not talk to these people in this office, because that's a biggish office. Not biggish. It's a pretty big office where four or five people can sit at a table and have a meeting, a conversation. I don't know what they discussed, but I was just told that they were supposed to be released and driven to Belgrade. To who, where, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: According to your description, there was never any mention of any arrangements being made beforehand, and there was also no description of him ordering you to do anything. He came to ask you permission and you gave it to him; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never gave me any orders. He never came before. He only came that morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Let's go back to the meetings that you had with the other detainees. You have told investigators of the Prosecutor that you ate fresh and healthy food when you were working at the KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that everybody ate fresh and healthy food, because in the warehouses, not too much food was ever stockpiled, so it could not be old or past its expiry date. I never felt any consequences as a result of the fact that I ate that food, so I consider it to be healthy and fresh. And that is very important for the human organism, for food to be healthy and fresh, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But you knew, from what the detainees were telling you, that they did not receive enough food to eat; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, please, don't. I keep saying that no one ever told me that they were not receiving enough food to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Isn't it true that [redacted] told you that there should be the food -- the leftover food should be given to the detainees? And as a doctor, he said the food wouldn't spoil, but that they didn't have enough food, so they were willing to eat even leftovers. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to understand two things here. During the first days, detained persons got food from the kitchen of the military that was at Livade, and of course, it might have happened - I did not see it happen - that food that was not eaten was thrown out of the containers that it was brought in. However, I never heard of any surplus food from our kitchen being thrown away, and I did not hear from any detainee that he had too little food, because three meals is three meals, after all. I cannot assert this, and I was not in charge of monitoring that, but it is possible that perhaps there was not always enough, perhaps, but none of the detained persons complained that they did not get enough food.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, on the 6th of June, 2000, during your interview with investigators - this is on page 35 in the English version of Exhibit P46 - you stated: "On one occasion [redacted] said that the food should not be thrown away, that it should be preserved for the following day. I replied, `Doctor, if the food is preserved for the following day, it's going to rot. It's going to be spoiled, and one should not give such rotten, spoiled food for people to eat.' And he said, `It won't hurt them.'"

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the days were hot and freezers and refrigerators were not working, that is correct, from my point of view, that the food would spoil. But I told you, most probably, because afterwards, never. When the kitchen started working within the compound of the KP Dom, no one ever told me that food was thrown away when they brought it from Livade, from the kitchen where they did the cooking for the army as well, because during the first days, I cannot state with certainty, but until the kitchen started working at the KP Dom, food was brought from Livade where it was prepared for the military as well, and that is where the command of the rear was too. That is this area called Livade. That is where these warehouses are, too, where the food was kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, wasn't it obvious to you, based on the conversation that you had with [redacted], that the detainees did not have enough food to eat and that's why he was asking that food be kept for the following day? Wasn't that the only conclusion you could draw from that kind of request?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not conclude that it was that way. My conclusion was, rather, that he wanted it to be used economically so that there would be no waste, so that food would be used economically. Not that somebody did not have enough food, because I cannot imagine that somebody was that inhuman not to give people food and to spill it, on the other hand, to throw it away. Because I thought that they did not feel it necessary to use all that food and that perhaps that's why it was thrown away, although I didn't know about it. I can't say now that the doctor did not say the truth, but I must say that I heard a lot of things when he appeared here that caused great concern, in my opinion, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Isn't it true that during this interview when you told the investigators what I just quoted, the question that was asked of you was: Did [redacted] complain about the food? And that was the answer that you gave. It wasn't whether you had any discussions about food management or the use of resources, but it was about whether he complained about the food, and in fact the conversation you had was him complaining about the food; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And he said that it should not be thrown away. But my conclusion was in that sense, that he wanted, from the point of view of good husbandry, that no food should be thrown away. That's how everybody should think. And perhaps the food had already gone bad, because if it had stayed in that kind of dish overnight, that was closed in these dishes where it was brought, perhaps it could have gone a bit sour. And most probably the cooks came to the conclusion that this food should be thrown away rather than given to people which could have caused a disease or something, and I think that that would have been a far greater misfortune if somebody got dysentery or some other kind of abdominal ailment. Nowadays also I throw away food that I'm not sure about. It's better to throw it away than to risk something. If you see that it's not tasty, it's better to eat plain bread than to eat other things as well and then get an upset stomach and get sick.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, when you met with your former colleague, RJ, in your office, he asked for food that you had left over in your office; Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. right? He asked for it to be taken back to his room so he could eat it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm not aware of that at all, and I'm so surprised that my colleague said that. I do not remember something like that at all, that something like that had happened and that he had asked for that, because I personally think that had he asked me for that, that I would have obtained some tinned food through the warehouse keeper for my colleague. I simply can't believe this. Why did my colleague say that? Well, let it be. That is his affair. But I really cannot remember that that took place, nor do I remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you never saw Muslims walking around in the yard for exercise; right? The only time they were in the yard was going to and from the canteen for meals; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that at times I did, but it was very seldom that I saw them going for a meal. The rest, I never even looked at that yard except when passing by on my way to the furniture factory - and that was very seldom - and the dining-room. And through the window -- I didn't look through the window into the yard. Very seldom. No, I can't remember ever casting a deliberate look, unless it was as I would be standing up and then I just cast a glimpse. But yes, they could walk around without my seeing them, because my office overviews the facilities where they are accommodated rather than the playground beyond the dining-room and towards the furniture factory. So perhaps it did happen that I had a look at these facilities, accommodation facilities, but not that I walked to my window to look through it with a purpose in mind deliberately, because that is the position of the windows in the room, so that they could walk without my seeing them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So in other words, your windows from the warden's office faced directly onto the prisoners' quarters rather than the yard; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Especially where there was this desk. Yes, precisely. That is how you could see, from that desk. And that is the central part of the building, not that one more to the left which is, I think, building number 1 on your sketches or what. But that is the building where the clinic was there. It couldn't be seen from my window, through that window which was next to the desk, as far as I can remember the arrangement of the view.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And just so we're clear about what the view was from the warden's office, I'd like to have you shown Exhibit 6/2, P6/2.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think I made a mistake. The warden's office, because it's on the second floor, it should be 6/3.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, could you show us -- you've given us a description now of what you could see from your office. Could you show us now what you could see, just so we're very clear about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- no. I thought you were showing something to me. I think that this is my office, my office, where the pointer is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, I understand that at one point you had an office on the ground floor and then you moved -- in the early days, and then you moved upstairs to the warden's office on the second floor. The place you're pointing to now, is that the ground floor office or the second floor office? I know this is a floor plan for the second floor, but I want to be clear about the location of the office you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pointing this thing that you have given me, that is, the ground floor of the second floor [as interpreted]. Do you agree or will you give me another ground plan? But I can also explain on this one. I can explain the first office and the second office with this plan. The first office is on the ground floor, where, according to others, was the censorship, and the second office, the second warden's office, was on the second floor of the administrative building. And you told me that this is the second floor. So my office -- my office in the administrative building is this one here. And the desk was here, in this part, next to this wall, the desk.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'll just describe this for the record. The witness is pointing to -- it would be the far left side of the right-hand wing of that office. So if you come into the KP Dom, it's directly to the right of the entrance but on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's also the room that almost every other witness in the place has identified as the warden's office. I think we can move on from this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to have the record reflect that the place where the desk is indicated by this witness is precisely that wall on the extreme left-hand side of the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krnojelac, could you show us what your visibility was from that room if you look out the window?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what I'm saying, that this building, this guard building, protrudes slightly, and somehow during the construction it penetrated the yard, so that I couldn't see this part from my office, especially this part here, from this office that I had. That is, I could see something in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The witness, when he said that he could not see, he pointed in the direction of what's been indicated as Room 13, but what he could see was more in the direction of Room 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, please, to add just that it depends whether I sat down or stood up. If I sat at the desk, then I couldn't see anything, because this view was obstructed because of what is below the window, and one could not see anything from the sitting position. And it was only if I had stood up and was upright that I could see it, but not this part that I showed you before. So you must understand me. It depends on whether I was sitting down or whether I was in an upright position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krnojelac. And isn't it true that from one of the windows in that warden's office there was the barrel of a machine-gun that pointed out precisely over the prisoners' quarters, and this was the machine-gun gun that RJ asked you about when he visited your office, and you told him that it was only a barrel but it was there to scare the detainees? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say under full responsibility that there was absolutely no pipe and nobody ever asked me about it. There was no barrel, when I was asked. But when he laughed, I decided by his laughter, I decided that he had made it up or that somebody had made him say that, because I don't believe it. But I am affirming that there was no barrel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need this diagram any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Are you saying that RJ made the comment about the machine-gun but there was no machine-gun even when he talked about it, that he just randomly made a comment that there was a machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Come out of the question. Machine-guns, or any barrels. There was no barrel. I guarantee that. Nothing like that in my office, but if I made add, this censorship, that is the first office, my view was even more obstructed there. My view was even more obstructed from the censorship office. Because you mentioned which room it was about, and I'm explaining it. From the censorship even less, because of the window and because of the device which was next to the window and because of another window, the -- my field of vision was even smaller.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Are you saying, when you talked about RJ, that he did make a comment about the machine-gun and then laughed about it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During his presentation, when I watched him, that was my impression and my conclusion, but I'm saying that it was not in the office, and I do say it under full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Krnojelac is: Did RJ make a comment about the machine-gun when he was in your office?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no. There was no conversation about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, during the winter between 1992 and 1993, there was no heating in the prisoners' quarters of the KP Dom; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the area where the detainees were accommodated, what I'm saying is that from time to time, I would see smoke coming out of the chimney. Now, what rooms did the smoke come from, do I not know, but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there was smoke coming out of the chimney.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And was this smoke from wood burning? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, in furnaces using firewood, like the one that existed in my administrative building. There was this stove, and we used firewood for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: There were some -- there was one room in the prisoners' quarters that was used for convicted Serb prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The distribution of those quarters for people serving the sentences pronounced on them before the conflict, if you mean those persons, yes, there was this room, but I do not know exactly which, because I've never been there, as I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You were in charge, you told us, of those people serving their sentences, and you're telling us that you never visited them in their room to see how they were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never went to visit them, because they had others. As I said, late Novica had assumed full responsibility. After that, he tasked the Rehabilitating Officer Zecevic, so that I didn't. And those who came now and then to use alcohol, because I said, and I think you understand when I say that at the farm, it was a semi-open institution. There was alcohol, so -- yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, the question was not about the farm. We've talked about the farm. My question was about the KP Dom compound and about the people serving their sentences who were housed in the KP Dom. You were in charge of those people; right? Not Mr. Mujovic and Mr. Zecevic who were in charge at the farm. You were responsible, according to your own words, for those people serving sentences, and so you were responsible for those people serving sentences who were indeed housed at the KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except that another person was responsible for them, for those who were either in KP Dom. It was Mr. Lazo Divljan who was responsible for them, and he used them for work.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You were, nevertheless, responsible for their welfare, right, to make sure that they had enough to eat, that they were kept warm, that they were treated humanely. That was still your responsibility; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. But nobody -- none of them ever complained to me about having take a bath, about not having heating or food like everybody else accommodated in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You put in measures to make sure that they had enough to eat and that they were kept warm and that they could be treated humanely; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not take any special measures, because I'd already said in the beginning, but I was a teacher and I knew a little about it. And it was people who had spent some time in the KP Dom who would know these things, and they simply came to meet me halfway because of all the circumstances and all my troubles, and they just came to help me in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The prisoners serving their sentences had access to television and radio, right, while they were detained or imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean this period of time that I was there, I wouldn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yet Husein Lojo, a Muslim teacher who came and spoke with you, asked you for TV and radio, and you said you couldn't provide it to him; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that I could provide it for him. Excuse me. I said that it was jurisdiction of the military command, and they are the ones who can provide it and that they should provide it, not me, because how could I provide it for them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You also knew that the Muslim detainees didn't have access to visitors. They were not permitted visitors after the first few weeks; right? In other words, in May of 1992, they were allowed visitors, but then after that, nobody could receive visitors from the outside. You knew that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, they did not -- that they did not receive visitors, except for a few days when it was said that they had contracted lice, and it was then that visits were prohibited. After that, I do not recall any prohibition of visits, nor do I know who could have prohibited those visits. If the visits were prohibited, then this prohibition could only come from the military command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You also knew that the Serbs serving their sentences were allowed to walk around in the KP Dom compound, right, while the Muslim prisoners were detained in their rooms?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had no contact with them either. Then I did not know it. The internal organisation, either in the case of ones or the case of others was not something that I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, on behalf of the Serb prisoners serving their sentences, you wrote recommendations for their early release based on the work that they did at the farm; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean persons serving sentences.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: That was precisely my question.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was done beforehand, too, but since people knew more about that, I told you, those people who worked there, and they made the list and the report, the analysis for the Ministry of Justice, they thought that they should write who would be -- who was eligible for -- for some lenience at different periods of time, and it had to do with their conduct and the way in which they performed their tasks at the farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like to have the witness shown Exhibit D85. The first page of the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: This is a document that you prepared, Mr. Krnojelac, listing the persons serving their sentences, and for each one -- for most of them you've made a recommendation for a reduction in sentence because of the work done and the behaviour of the individual; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I just said that. I did not write this, but I accept it from my collaborators, this information which they had written.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You never prepared any sort of documents like this on behalf of the Muslim detainees; right? There was never any review of their sentences based on their acceptable behaviour, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excellent question, and my answer to it is as follows: For things that I was responsible for, I had to do something like this and authorise it, but all those in the Ministry of Justice knew, they had been told verbally, and they told me that this could be done by persons who worked with persons serving sentences, and I was responsible for them. And for those other persons, because I was not responsible for them, I could not make any proposals for those persons who were detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: As far as you know, there were never any documents like this -- I'm not asking you if you did it yourself. You've already told us that you did not. But as far as you know, nobody ever prepared documents like this regarding the Muslim detainees; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I do not know if anybody did that. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Nobody ever came to you to ask you about the work that the detainees did for the furniture factory or the farm or the metalwork shop and whether the detainees did acceptable work that could go toward their early release; right? Nobody ever asked you about that, did they?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither did anyone ask me nor had anyone reason to ask me, because those people knew that I was not responsible for their work --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because there was somebody else who was responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: My question was: You've told us that you were in charge ultimately of the furniture factory and the farm and the metal workshop. And you've also told us that Muslim detainees worked in all three of those places. And my question to you is: No one ever came to you to ask you about the performance of those Muslim detainees for the purposes of reviewing whether they should be released; right? No one ever asked you for your opinion about the work they did; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody asked me for my opinion, but whether heads, work units were asked about that, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You're saying that even though you were the person who was ultimately in charge of those three economic units, that nobody asked you in your official capacity but might possibly have asked someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever turned to me with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, during one of your conversations with your former colleague RJ, he told you that he could hear the sound of people being beaten; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleague, my highly appreciated colleague, never said that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: He never told you that people were scared when they heard these beatings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never, ever talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Didn't RJ also tell you about a specific incident when one detainee tried to get ahead in the line to get food and was beaten by guards because he did that? Did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I am telling you that he did not, and I do not recollect that there was any conversation with my colleague about this or any other similar situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You asked RJ to give you information about what the detainees' conditions were like, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, not even that. I never told him even that, nor did he ever tell me about that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: RJ was a colleague of yours, a close colleague, for many years at the school; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very close colleagues, colleagues of many years. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You were friends with him in addition to being colleagues; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a sense, friendly colleagues, because if we are colleagues, then we're friends too. We didn't visit one another at home - that is, we did not carry out our friendship in our homes - but in school, outings with children, excursions, or in pubs, and so we would spend some time as friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: He was someone you trusted; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is not the only one. There are a number of people whom I trusted, and he was one of those that, yes, whom I trusted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During the times that you met when he was detained at the KP Dom, you sometimes talked about what was happening at the KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He never said to me or talked to me about what was going on, except that we would sit down, have some coffee, and talk. And yes, there was frequent mention of his -- the state of his health, and that is how that medicine came up, what the colleague mentioned. It was really very difficult to find that medicine in the area, but he managed to get it from somewhere - whether from Serbia or Montenegro, I don't know - but she [as interpreted] found somewhere that medicine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you never asked RJ how he was doing? Aside from his health, you never asked him about what life was like for him in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever he came to see me, he was always in such a good mood that there was no problem. He had taken care of his family, he knew where his children were, where his wife was. So on the contrary; he always seemed to be in a very good mood - that's the way he seemed to me - like he did before the war. He was generally in a good mood.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You told him sometimes about things that you knew that had happened at the KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep repeating this to you. I did not know. I never talked to him and he never talked to me about these things that were going on, if they were going on, because I do not know that they were going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You knew that Halim Konjo had died at the KP Dom and you told RJ about it, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that he had died. I heard that he had committed suicide, and it was only natural that I should tell my colleague about that, because there was no reason for me to hide that. I found that out through Mr. Jokanovic, that a commission came and that he committed suicide. I did not hide this. With your permission, may I say that I never hid anything that I knew, or rather, what I heard from others in terms of what they conveyed to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When Halim Konjo died at the KP Dom, that news spread very quickly that very morning; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying once again: He didn't die. I heard that he committed suicide. I don't know whether it was that morning, that same morning. I mean, I found out after the commission had already come, or rather, after the commission had finished its work. That's when I found out from Gojko Jokanovic that a commission came because of the suicide of Mr. Konjo. I don't know anything more about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you learned about that the very morning after Mr. Konjo died; right? You told the investigators during your June 6th, 2000 interview, on page 38 in the English version: "When I came to work in the morning, I found out about that case."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I'm telling you how I found out. Mr. Jokanovic said to me that he had committed suicide and that a commission came to carry out an investigation. Whether it was immediately in the morning, at 7.00, or whether it was at 9.00, or when the commission came, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you stated further on that same page: "It happened in the morning. During the change of guards, the word was spread that it had taken place." So the news of Mr. Konjo's death spread very quickly that same morning after he died, right, and you heard about it then as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said now how I found out about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. RJ also told you that people were disappearing overnight, didn't he, that sometimes detainees were taken out and no one ever heard from them again?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never said that to me, or am I aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During your conversations with [redacted], he also told you that the Muslim detainees required medical attention, medical treatment; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. [redacted] did not talk to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: [redacted] never mentioned to you that the detainees needed medical attention?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The pharmacy that you said was a part of the Drina Economic Unit served both Muslim detainees and Serbs serving their sentences; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You did not make any distinction in the distribution of medicines between those two groups, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I said that I gave the key to Mr. Jokanovic, then I did not distribute the medicines either. He distributed the medicines, and I never told him to make any kind of distinction. I told him to give medicine to everyone for as long as there was enough medicine, or rather, in line with what the doctor would prescribe.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the time when Ekrem Zekovic escaped from the KP Dom in July of 1993. During that time, you were still working at the KP Dom, you've told us, and when you found out that he escaped, this concerned -- this worried you, didn't it, that someone should have escaped directly from the metalwork shop, of which you were ultimately responsible; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask you kindly to say the following: Already then I was working on the preparations for the handover of my job, because I knew by then that I had been discharged, or rather, that I had received a decision stating that I was no longer warden, and it is precisely for that reason that I called Relja that morning so that we could go to Brod in order to settle our debts and finish all the other business that we had at Brod, business that he was familiar with. Relja and I went to Brod. We completed this business and we asked if there were some other outstanding problems to have all of this prepared as soon as possible. And I had no duties involved with his escape from the metalwork shop. It's not that I was sad, so that I could say that I was sad that he had escaped, but there's just one thing: I would have felt sorry had he gotten killed, but that was his right, I imagine, to try to escape if he had the opportunity to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Relja Goljanin was still in charge of the metalwork shop at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relja Goljanin was still in charge of the metalwork shop. In this period while I was there, it was called the metalwork shop. It's still called the metalwork shop. But it was the metalwork shop before too, and it was also the plant for maintenance of various things at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You and Mr. Goljanin were at Brod that very day when Mr. Zekovic escaped; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Zoran Sekulovic had not started working, had not been appointed the warden yet at that point; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal opinion is that they would not have given me discharge papers without giving others -- or somebody else an appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'm not asking --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was being discharged --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'm not asking your opinion; I'm asking you about facts. When Mr. Zekovic escaped, Zoran Sekulovic had not started as the new warden yet; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He hadn't come to the KP Dom yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And there was nobody who was appointed as some sort of acting warden between you and him; right? You remained in your position as warden until Mr. Sekulovic started as warden; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that anyone else was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So when you and Mr. Goljanin found out that in your absence one of the detainees escaped from the metalwork shop, this was naturally something that concerned you; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not concerned. Relja had told me that Zeka had escaped from the metalwork shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And since you were technically the superior to Mr. Goljanin and the metalwork shop, this also concerned you; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not concern me, because it is the security that is supposed to take care of that. Why is it called security? They should secure things and make sure that nobody can escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When Mr. Zekovic was brought back the next day, you were waiting for his arrival at the KP Dom gate, weren't you? When he was brought back, you saw him immediately; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not waiting and I did not see him immediately. At that time I had finished my work at the accounting service, or rather, that part of my work that I was supposed to complete, and I was supposed to go home. And in the hall, after 30 or 40 metres, in that part where you enter, where the main entrance is to the hall, I saw a small group of people, and they took a man somewhere behind that entrance office, the guard's office at the entrance. And I said, "What was going on?" and then I was told, "The police captured Zekovic and they brought him right behind the guard office." Since this was the end of working hours, and since I knew that I had received the decision stating that I was no longer warden, I asked the guard on duty whether I could see him, and he said, "Yes, you can." And I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. walked in there and there was a guard in front of the office - I can't remember which one - and I said, "The duty officer said that I could go see him." And he opened the door and I saw him sitting on the bed. I offered him a cigarette and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: We'll get to that. Mr. Krnojelac, when Mr. Zekovic was being brought in, one of the guards bringing him in was Burilo, right, Milenko Burilo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me that I cannot remember at all who was on duty then and which guards were in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But you do know Milenko Burilo, don't you, who he is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment I can't remember which guards were there and whether Burilo was there. I'm not saying that he was there or that he wasn't there. I'm saying I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'm asking you not about that date in particular but whether you know the guard Milenko Burilo at all. You recognise him; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Burilo before the war as well. Not particularly, but I knew him, and I knew that he worked at the KP Dom as a guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Isn't it true that even before the war he had a reputation for being violent toward prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of that because I did not work on that during the war, and I was not asking people who was what kind of person or worker in some other organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During your interview with investigators on the 13th of July of 2000, on page 40 in the English version, 36 in B/C/S, you describe Burilo as being sturdy, corpulent, and strong. Do you remember that description?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I remember that description? I don't know, but I do know that he was strong, on the fair side. He had sort of reddish hair, if you could put it that way, but he was a strong, corpulent man and kind of plumpish. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you know that he was a guard during this time, right, at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, he worked at the KP Dom security. I mean if you are asking me about that day in particular, I can't remember, but while I was there, I would see him amongst the KP Dom security men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You told the investigators, regarding Burilo, on that same page: "I don't know what he had with these people before the war, and I especially don't know what he did during the war." But you knew that he was a policeman at the KP Dom during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I agree and that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When Ekrem Zekovic was brought in, isn't it true that Burilo beat him at the entrance and that you and the guard Milivoj Milic had to step in and try to get him to stop beating him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reason for me not to say the way things actually were. In the meantime, I had taken some 30 steps in the hall, and I did not see that. I only saw that they took him by the entrance, the room for guards on duty, by that room. And then I don't know who was there exactly. They brought Zeka. And I already told you about this. I asked, and I went there, and I saw him sitting there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Mr. Zekovic was unconscious when he was first brought into that room because he had been beaten upon arrival?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came, I found him sitting on the bed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: One of the reasons you gave us for wanting to see Mr. Zekovic was, according to your testimony here, that you thought perhaps he had gotten beaten. So you understood that there was a distinct possibility, when someone tried to escape, that he would in fact get beaten when he was caught; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I asked the officer on duty to see him, it is true that I asked to see what condition he was in, physical and mental, and to chat to him as a person, to smoke a cigarette together, to give him some relief, perhaps, with that cigarette. Had I known -- I did not know, because there were not such cases. I was not aware of any such case. It was the first such case of a Muslim detainee trying to escape. But I did hear that before, there were two escapes of Serbs who had been detained at the KP Dom, that they escaped from the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You knew, when you requested to see Mr. Zekovic, that there was a very good possibility he would have been beaten when he was captured; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that. I simply wanted to see him and to smoke a cigarette together with him. Did I know? No, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You didn't know Mr. Zekovic very well, did you, before he came to KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You didn't have very much contact with him while you were at the KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I even don't know whether I had a single contact with him. I can't remember. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So this is somebody with whom you had no special relationship; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And yet you specifically requested a guard to go see this Muslim detainee after he was captured; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You told Mr. Zekovic, when you met him in the cell, that it was too bad that he had tried to escape, because otherwise he would have been on a list of people to be released that very day; right? "That day" being the --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's not right. I did not say anything to Mr. Zekovic about that. I just asked him, "How are you? Are you all right? Would you like to smoke a cigarette?" I offered him a cigarette, and he said, "I'm fine." I offered him a cigarette and he took the cigarette and we both lit cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: This was -- Mr. Zekovic wasn't surprised to see you, was he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't know. I cannot know what other people feel. He only surprised me with his statement here when he told me that I gave him a Herzegovina cigarette. Believe me, I never smoked Herzegovina cigarettes in all my life. Had he mentioned any other brand of cigarette, I would have believed it, but he specifically remembers Herzegovina, and I know that I never ever smoked Herzegovina. And now as for his other feelings, whether he felt this way or that way, I don't know, because I cannot assess other people's feelings.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I should have asked it this way: He did not act surprised to see you, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, believe me, I didn't notice any special surprise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You didn't have to introduce yourself; right? He knew who you were?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not introduce myself. I believe he did know. He said that he went to the metalwork shop, so he saw me and he knew. And he probably knew me before the war, before the armed conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The day that this conversation took place was the 8th of July, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember the date. It was in the month of July, at any rate, 1993. That's when he escaped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to show you Defence Exhibit D45. This is a list of Muslims to be released from the KP Dom, signed by the Foca Tactical Group Commander, Colonel Marko Kovac. It's a list of people dated the 12th of July, 1993, and it says that they are to be released on the order of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska of July 8, 1993, for an exchange. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Zekovic's name is not on this list. That's clear; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for what I see here, I don't see his name here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But this is precisely the decision that you were referring to or that was referred to by Mr. Zekovic when he said that you told him on that date that he would have been on the list but because he escaped, he was not on the list any more; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that I did not say that to him, nor did I know of this exchange or this list at all. And we see where this decision was made and where this list was made and who signed it as well. I can't see here on the monitor, but there must be a signature there who signed it, who approved of this exchange. I did not know about this. I didn't know about a single one, for that matter. If ever I found out about an exchange, I found out only after it had actually happened, never in advance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need this document any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you said that this cigarette that you offered Mr. Zekovic was a peace pipe. Can you explain why a peace pipe was necessary? What kind of peace were you trying to achieve with him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember having said a peace pipe, but perhaps I compared that cigarette. If one smokes a cigarette together, that is some kind of cooperation, nice cooperation, but I didn't refer to those peace pipes that people talk about in this world. I was thinking of tranquility, because I thought, I thought that perhaps he was frightened, that he was scared somehow at that moment. And as for his momentary psychological situation, perhaps it might have been easier for him. Because when I light a cigarette, when I go to the cell now afterwards, I inhale four or five times and I almost eat up the cigarette. No. In no other way this peace pipe, only in terms of getting more tranquil, from a health point of view, because we all tend to get upset and these are problems. And of course this is more harmful than it is good in terms of bringing us tranquility, but it's a habit that a person acquires.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You were trying to get Mr. Zekovic tranquil so you could find out about the circumstances of his escape; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not remember that we talked about anything else but which way he had gone, where he spent that night. And he explained this to me, that he crossed the Drina, that on the right bank of the Drina he spent the night, and that in the morning he set out in that direction to see his family. I didn't even know. He told me then that his family was in Montenegro. We did not talk about anything else then. We each smoked a cigarette. I left. The guard stayed there. And what happened later, well, I just went to the apartment where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: It's 11.00, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, none of the prison guards or staff was ever punished for their treatment of Ekrem Zekovic after his escape; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you or any other staff members suffer any consequences from the fact that he was able to escape? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not know. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to turn our attention to the Red Cross. The Red Cross did not have access to the KP Dom until the 23rd of June, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, and from, I heard from others, they had come before that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: They had attempted to come into the KP Dom, but you never permitted them to come inside; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never turned to me or asked me to gain access, so who it was who banned them from entering, who prohibited access to them, I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You had contact with the Red Cross as early as October of 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the exact time when that happened, but be that as it may, I only -- I had contacted with them only once, or rather, twice, is that I had a kind of contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to have you shown Exhibit D106. This is a letter dated 21st October 1992 which you signed, as the warden, to the Red Cross in Foca, asking for aid packages for captured and detained persons. That's your signature and you wrote this; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one explanation: I did not know that you are talking about this Red Cross, not the International Red Cross. Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: There was a difference, in your mind, between the Red Cross in Foca and the International Red Cross? Isn't it the same organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my mind, it is one and the same, but just to make this distinction so that it wouldn't turn out as if I hadn't had any contact with the Red Cross in Foca. Yes, this is indeed my signature and request addressed to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you testified in your direct examination that in fact you did not receive these aid packages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive these packages, but a few days later I received another kind of foodstuffs than those that were in the packages. At least, that's what I heard, because the head of the Red Cross said that she could not get those packages because at that time the refugees had turned out, and those packages were very convenient for refugees and displaced, so that later on she gave -- I wouldn't know the quantities, but there was some oil and beans and some detergents, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you got foodstuffs not from the Red Cross itself, right, but from another source? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That food that I am referring to came from the warehouse which belonged to the Red Cross, where they stocked this food which was received by aid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You made a distinction between the Foca Red Cross and the International Red Cross. The Foca Red Cross contact you had was with a former student of yours; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Which was different from the International Red Cross, in your mind, because those people from the International Red Cross were from a different country and spoke a different language; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but because the International Red Cross did not communicate with me; they communicated with the army and the army command. And about this here, I directly communicated with the boss of the Red Cross. That is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And just looking at document D106 again, under the subject line, these were aid packages that you requested for captured and detained persons, not for sentenced people, not for the people serving their sentences; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "detained persons," I also meant persons who had been sentenced and were serving their terms. I meant them just as well as those persons who had been brought in under custody.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So it was for everybody who was held at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any event, yes, I wrote them and asked for it for everybody in the same way, with no discrimination whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. With the assistance of the usher, I'd like to have you shown document D37. Mr. Krnojelac, document D37 was submitted by the Defence, and it is a report from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Justice and Administration and the Section for Enforcement of Sentences, to the Minister of the Ministry of Justice and Administration. It's dated the 22nd of October, 1992, and it's the report on the situation in prisons and prisoner of war collection camps. And it's several pages long, listing several prison camps, and it says that it was based on a list given by the International Red Cross. The Foca KP Dom is not listed on this document, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking through it. KP Dom Foca. No, I don't see it mentioned. This report was submitted by Slobodan Avlijas, not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, the people who were detained at the KP Dom Foca were not registered with the International Red Cross by the time of this document; right? That's why it's not listed.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply do not know whether they were registered or not, because they were not under my jurisdiction. If they were not, then it is the responsibility of the military command, that is, the Tactical Group. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, this report was prepared by the Ministry of Justice and it is addressed to the Minister of Justice. You often went to Ministry of Justice meetings in Bijeljina; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I wouldn't -- that word "often." It was only two or three times that I went, and I must say that at none of -- that none of those meetings that I attended took place anywhere else but in Bijeljina, because in Bijeljina, there was, but you'll begrudge me repeating it all the time, because there was a detachment or a subsidiary or something, because it was sort of a halfway for everybody to come, to go, and that is why we all went to Bijeljina where those meetings were held.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And in fact, you had just -- there had just been a meeting in Bijeljina in September of 1992 where prosecutors, judges, and wardens were all called together to discuss cooperation with the military judicial organs; isn't that right? Weren't you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the exact dates of the meetings, but I think that there should be some orders, because at a meeting in 1992, I was present there and there were some justice authorities or the presidents of courts were also present at that meeting and wardens of KP -- different penitentiary institutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And at that time, there was a discussion about these so-called prisoners of war camps within the Justice Ministry; right? There was some discussion within the Justice Ministry of these prisoners of war camps; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the discussion was not about prisoners of war or persons brought under custody at the time but about the distribution about penitentiaries and the work of courts, rather, justice authorities in municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: With the military justice organs; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember them being present there or any discussions between the justice authorities and the military. It was with civilian authorities, that is, with bodies of civilian courts, of civil courts, whatever you like to call them. Courts, not military, not military ones. At least as I can remember. Or at least nobody introduced himself and said that he came from a military court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to have the witness shown Exhibit D89.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: This is a notice set out by the Ministry of Justice and Administration, dated the 5th of September, 1992, and it states that the Ministry of Justice has assessed the situation and concluded that a working meeting must be convened with court presidents, public prosecutors, and wardens, and that includes you, right, Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't even read this document properly because I think my glasses are too poor and I can't read this. And I cannot remember that I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ever knew about this document or that I know anything about it. No. No, I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo, it could be increased in size on the screen, I think, if you wanted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: We can certainly do that, Your Honour. We could ask the usher to please help us by putting the B/C/S version on the screen, and then we can ask the audio-visual staff to increase the size. The relevant part would be the first four paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When I see the document that the accused was looking at, I can see I'd have some trouble myself, and I believe my glasses are all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, does this help? Are you now able to read the document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember this document. I do not remember ever seeing it or receiving it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: In the course --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can't, I can't read it because -- but I simply do not remember at least the heading which I did read, but this heading I did read. The rest I didn't read. I don't remember ever being informed about such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Let's try it this way, Mr. Krnojelac: This is the copy that we got from your lawyers and we don't have anything that's any clearer than this, but we did manage to get it translated by the translation staff here, and I will read a portion of it to you in English and ask you questions based on that. You've told us you don't know this document, but it's true that you did attend a working meeting that was called by the Ministry of Justice after the 5th of September, 1992, the purpose of which meeting was to discuss cooperation with various other judicial organs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that any of those meetings we held discussed such a document. I simply do not remember. It was a long time ago. I do not remember. Perhaps I was there and present, but it had nothing to do with the KP Dom, as I was a beginner in all this and perhaps I didn't pay attention, and so that is why I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, I don't -- I'm not focusing the questions about whether you know about the document. The question was your participation in a meeting. I'm going to read from the document, from the English version, and just ask you about the statement. According to this document signed by the Minister or signed for the Minister of Justice: "Wardens of penal and correctional facilities are required to bring to the meeting the rules of internal organisation for approval." That was what you were instructed to do and that's what you did; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that rules were adopted by one of those meetings. I brought to that meeting the rules on the internal organisation that existed before, prior to the armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: According to this document, this meeting took place on the 16th of September, 1992, and that attendance was mandatory. So you did participate; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm the date, whether it was that date, but such a meeting which was to adopt the rules on the internal organisation of work, I said that I had brought the rules, but I had brought the rules which had been adopted before the armed conflict. We never prepared any rules, and they accepted those rules which were the old rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Among the other things that were discussed at this meeting were cooperation between the civilian military -- civilian judicial organs and the military judicial organs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember any military organs at that meeting where I presented these rules. I do not remember any military bodies being at that meeting, or perhaps I did not know them, and I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Again, this is not my question whether there was any military people present, but let me read to you a portion of paragraph 4: "This notice of a meeting requires the presidents of the high courts and senior public prosecutors to prepare briefings." And on paragraph 4 it states that among other things, the briefings should include information about cooperation with the internal affairs organs, military judicial organs, inspection services, et cetera.
