utterances.text: Well, agreed in the sense that this upper part of the KP Dom does not have any lighting, it is unguarded, so that it could be a kind of protection, both -- also of the property which was in this part, right above, right behind the area serving for the accommodation of detained persons in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You could have written in an additional sentence in this request to say "in order to protect the property." You could have handwritten that in before you signed this, but you didn't do that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had I had my today's experience then, but after a month and a half, I didn't have all that experience. Had I had my today's experience, I suppose I would have done that, but a man has no experience, has no knowledge, has no expertise. And presumably, I suppose, at that moment it did not occur to me. But thank you very much. Yes, that would have been a good idea. But I couldn't really -- not everything could occur to me at that time. As for this first date, the 1st of June, that I signed it and wrote it, I put it to you that I did not. And I didn't know about the 1st of June, although it says so here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, what was the reason for the mining, and who requested it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it transpires from this that that was requested by the army command, because they knew that 470 persons -- they knew how many guards they needed. And then from time to time -- and you also agree with me, and other witnesses also said that people went to stand guard. So that is that it often happened that there were not 42, but sometimes there were 31 or 30, depending on how many people had gone from the security to the front line, to the line of combat, if I may put it that way, and that is why I think that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, what was the reason for the mining?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I'm telling you, I did not write this, and I do not know what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You've told us today, just a moment ago, that the reason was to protect property. Are you saying that's not true?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I say something twice, then you tell me, "We've heard it. Don't go on." And when I say one thing once, then I'd rather not repeat it. One of the reasons, from my point of view, was also the protection of property.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you, in your capacity as the temporary warden, requested that these mines be put in because you had learned that somebody -- that the detainees might try to escape in early June; right? That's what happened. You signed this based on that information; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on that information, I am telling you that I didn't sign it. But it was brought, and I was told, "Milorad, you have to sign this document," and I signed it. I read it and signed it. And my only comfort was that because it was not lit and because it was not guarded, that it was also the protection of the KP Dom, and in no way because of this organisation. I had nothing to do with it, and it is obvious that it was the military who wrote it this way, because they were responsible and the guards were responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, there is nothing in this document that makes reference to the military making this request, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you think, and my view is what I've just explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: If there was a separate military command making this request to the War Presidency, there's no reason to ask for your signature, is there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, the entry and laying of mines precisely in a part of the KP Dom, property of KP Dom, they thought that that was the only way how they could enter and lay the mines.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: There is nothing in this document that says, "At the request of the military, I am giving permission for people to come lay mines." It says that, "As the warden, I am making the request for the mines to be brought in," right, or are you denying what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that I did not write it, that it was written by somebody else. It was written by a person who was -- who knew the situation at the KP Dom very well. And for me, after a month and a half, to know the situation all that well, after this period of time when one first had to take stock of the situation, and for me to know all this, that I knew all that, well, had I been a warden to this day, I wouldn't have known about this thing. But there are people who knew that, and they wrote that, and they did not write it because of me, nor did I write it. And I am telling you, that is how it was, and it's up to you to decide what's more convenient to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, after you read and signed this document, you knew exactly what weapons there were at the KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know where these weapons come from, whether these are the weapons that were received from the military command, or was it found in the KP Dom? I know that the armoury --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I didn't ask you where the weapons came from. I'm just saying that after you read this document and signed it on the 9th of June, 1992, you had knowledge of exactly what weapons there were at the KP Dom, right, because it's listed here.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never paid any attention to this: who, how much, what kind. I just cast a cursory glance. I wasn't interested to know what, where, who, whether it's in working order, whether it says we don't have ammunition, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And when you signed this letter, you agreed with the proposition that certain of the weapons be replaced with another kind of weapon which would be more effective and practical for guarding this number of prisoners at the KP Dom; right? That's what the final sentence of this letter says.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could only be to satisfy the guard commander for their security. I have nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: We'll move on. Mr. Krnojelac, you described --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: We don't need this document any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You described your life and you described how you come from a humble background; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you stated that when you were assigned to the school in Zavait in 1962, that was by decree; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you were -- when you had to fulfil your obligation to the army in 1963, that was also by decree, against your wishes; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had I had any other possibility, I wouldn't have gone to serve the army. I would have stayed and left my wife and army, so for me it's an obligation. It's a decree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Sir, the answer is simply yes. When you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not know why my learned friend asks the -- wants the witness to answer yes if she wants him to explain what she's asking. I also agree that we should move on, but if he feels that it is necessary to explain the answer, to say what is his view of that, I do not know why should he be denied that right and why he should be asked to answer only yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, your client concedes he talks too much, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and that is clearly right. Now, we've done nothing to interfere, but there does come a limit. That question could have been answered yes or no. If there is a need for an explanation, you have the right, in re-examination, to have that explanation given, but a cross-examiner is not obliged to let the witness have his head. Now, she's let him have his head throughout the last three days, and I think the time is coming when we're all getting tired. If the cross-examiner wants the witness to answer yes or no and it is a question which should be and could be answered yes or no, then she is entitled to have it. Now, you take it up in re-examination if you wish, but he's given that explanation at least twice, to my memory, already, and it wasn't necessary for him to say it. We're not fools. We can read the transcript. We know what he said, and it's unnecessary for it to be repeated every time. You proceed, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you went to pursue further studies in Sarajevo, you also described it as being under orders. You were ordered to go pursue those studies; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a shortage of mathematics and physics teachers, and I was told -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: It was not your choice, and you described it as being against your will; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was partly choice or, rather, willingness to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: As a result of this which you were ordered to do, you actually got a benefit; right? In other words, as a result of your pursuing these higher studies in Sarajevo, you were able to get a job in Foca rather than the rural towns where you previously taught; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there was also willingness from that point of view, so that I could send my children to high school. One has better chances when one is a mathematics and physics teacher than if one is only a primary schoolteacher, teaching Grades 1 through 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you were assigned to be the warden of KP Dom, you've described that as also having been an order against your will; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But you also got certain benefits from it. For example, you were not sent to the front line like everyone else, and your risks of being killed were greatly minimised; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's no privilege, because I already told you that I would have preferred to have been sent anywhere else, but I got orders to go to the KP Dom. That is only an aggravating circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: In addition, you had access to a car which you sometimes used for your personal use, not just for KP Dom business; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a family car. My son had a car for personal needs, so I did not need a car for personal needs. And it is mentioned only for -- the other vehicle's only mentioned for business needed by the Drina Economic Unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You got free labour to fix up your house from the Muslim detainees at the KP Dom, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is just a house that was protected. It was not being repaired. Until the present day, it has not been fully repaired. It was just protected from further dilapidation, and on somebody else's orders, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Labour was provided to you free. You never pay for that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever sent me a bill for that or an invoice.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: As a result of your having been the warden of KP Dom, you were promised another job within the justice -- within the municipality of Foca; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A job was not promised to me. Had it been promised to me, I would not have been unemployed for one year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: After the one year, during which time efforts were being made to find you a suitable position, you got a job in the Ministry of Education; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because again, a lot of work had to be done. It was not a question of resting up. Ten facilities had to be put in working condition so that the younger generations could receive a proper education. And not a single friend of mine went there to enjoy that kind of privilege.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During the year when you did not actually do any work, you still got credit for social security purposes; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most fortunately I didn't have to go and see a doctor, but I did have social insurance. That is why it says in that list from the KP Dom that it goes on until 1994, but I did not go to see a doctor a single time during that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And in fact, why when you finally got a job in September of 1994, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it was as headmaster of the school, which was a promotion; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was no promotion. I just wanted to be a teacher, and that is why in 1998, I did not reapply for the job of principal. But even had I applied, what happened, happened. But even the first time, it was orders. They said, "Here you are. If you want to, you can be principal. If not, nothing."

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: So again, a decision was placed to you in your life where you were ordered to do something against your will; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I was given a choice. "Take this or don't come back looking for another job and then try to make do on your own." And since I had no other way out, I had to accept that job too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You were given a choice that was not really a choice, so you were, according to your own description, ordered by decree to be headmaster; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much for having understood me precisely. That's just the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You see your life as a series of decisions that were made by other people, not by yourself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that that's the way it was in every respect. Most importantly, in my marriage, nobody else made decisions except for the two of us, and I have been most fortunate in that. As for the rest, there are quite a few cases where other people had a significant influence, because had I had any other choice, had I had some property or had I had a different trade that I could have been engaged in, I would have preferred going into agriculture than being principal of a school.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The way you see your life, and I'll just use one of the quotes that you gave us, "Everything that has happened to me except death." So you've been a victim all your life; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say all my life but a good part of my life. May I just mention this period to you, from the outbreak of the war conflict? My house burned down, my sons had that accident, my daughter-in-law -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: We've been through this litany of suffering that you've told us again and again about it and we know about it. That's why I asked you the question, to summarise it. You see your life as having been suffering at the hands of other people; right? That's a pattern. It's not your responsibility. These were things that you were forced to do by other people. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way it was in all segments. There were things that happened without that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You told us about your marriage. I know that that's an exception. You did that freely. But all the other things, the jobs, the things you were forced to do in your professional career, the misfortune that befell you and your family during the war, those were things that were outside your control, that somebody else was to blame; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether somebody else was to blame or not, I just wanted to add that you heard about my past, about my childhood, but those were good days, nice days, although there were hardships too. Then I worked. But I also had some good days, some fine days. I had my family too. Not everything was bad. During my life, there were nice days, good days, too, when a man enjoyed living in such a society and in such company. I cannot say that it's all dark when there were good things too. As for this, it was the way it was, except that I'm terribly pleased that I had people at the KP Dom who truly accepted the difficulties that I encountered as if they were their own, and they really helped me so that I would not have lost entirely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you knew the basic contents of the Geneva Conventions, right, that they were humanitarian laws about how detainees and prisoners had to be treated humanely; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had heard of them. But please try to understand me. I had nothing to do with the prisoners, but I tried, as much as I could, to help in any way so that it would be better from the point of view of food, means of hygiene, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, I'll quote your own words from the interview you gave to the investigators of the Prosecution's office regarding humane relations and humanitarian law. You said: "A person that possesses even a bit of soul has them already, so to speak, within himself." That's accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You didn't actually have to read any particular documents to know right from wrong and humane from inhumane. You already have that built in as a human being; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am clear with myself, that I do not have internal hatred towards other people, and if I will only work to help them, I believe that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is humane. But also, it is never a waste of time to read all these materials like the Geneva Conventions and everything else, because you never know when you may need that, as we can see. However, even had I read them, I could not do anything but what I have done because I was not in charge of the detained persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: These are not the questions. I am trying to go through the very last 15 minutes of the day in a very structured way, and you do not need to repeat what you have told us repeatedly already. So just please listen to the question and answer. When -- after your first day at the KP Dom and you saw the Muslim detainees there, you went home and you told your wife that you saw Muslim detainees at the KP Dom, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. On the first day, I did not go back home. I spent the night at the KP Dom. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The first night when you did go back, you told your wife that you saw Muslim detainees at the KP Dom, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came not home but to Cerezluk where I lived, I told her.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You told her -- you didn't tell her that they were suffering, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I only saw them through the window. How could I know that they were suffering and how they felt?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But you told your wife that you were not in charge of the Muslims, and you told her that to reassure her; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that to her because it was the Uzice Unit that was in charge of that, the unit that was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You also had frequent contact with Zarko Vukovic during the war; right? And he knew your role at the KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not frequent contacts, but there were contacts, and he knew what my role was. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you told him that you were concerned that you might be on the list of indicted persons by this Tribunal, he reassured you by saying that if you had been on the list -- that you were not on the list, because if you had been on the list, you would have already been arrested; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, where did you get that kind of information from? I never could have thought of this. It never could have crossed my mind that I could have come to the International Tribunal for having worked at the KP Dom. I don't see where you got this information from, because a man who does his job in an economic organisation, that he could come to answer for things he is not guilty of, I can't understand that. I'm sorry that I have to repeat this for the Honourable Court, but I was arrested. I had left my apartment and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Are you saying that you never told Zarko Vukovic that you were concerned that you might be on the list of indicted persons? You never said that to him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said this to him. I just said that if I knew that I was in any way a suspect, I would have gone immediately and voluntarily given myself up when Kunarac had surrendered. That's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You were already worried that you were on the list of indicted persons by the end of 1997; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never worried. I never thought that I could be accused or suspected, whichever way you want to put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to show you Exhibit P7, which is your ID, dated 1995. I'll give you the original and the photocopy can be placed on the ELMO. This is your identification card dated 11 January 1995, with your photograph; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And all the information contained in this document is accurate; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 25th of July, Stipe Stjepanovic [phoen], last in Birotici, Foca, Milorad Krnojelac. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'd like to have the witness shown Exhibit P8. Again, he can get the original and the photocopy can go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: This, Mr. Krnojelac, is an identification card, again with your photograph. It's a different photograph. It's issued from December 1st, 1997. And this shows a false name, Marko Kostic, with a false date of birth; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's just the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you carried both the real identification card and the false identification card with you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I explained why it was carried.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You told us that you were aghast when you received this false identification card, and yet, instead of putting it away or throwing it away, you carried it in your pocket and it was found on you on the date of your arrest; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was found on the day of the arrest. I carried both in my pocket.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you. We're done with these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you didn't care at all what happened to the Muslim detainees, did you? You didn't care at all what happened to them; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can you say that I didn't care? How able I was to know what was going on is another question, but I care about every person and I care about what's going on to any person. Because I lived in that kind of a milieu, and because of the children and because of the pupils, everyone was important to me, and their problems, and everything that had to do with their parents too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, I will quote to you from your interview with the investigators the 13th of July, 2000, and it's Exhibit P48. In the English it's page 36, lines 16 through 18, and in the B/C/S it's page 33, lines 3 through 6. You state: "I don't know what happened, what was in the civilian part, and in the final analysis, I don't care what was in the civilian part, just as I don't care what happened in the part controlled by the military, for which I was not responsible." It was all the same to you, wasn't it? You didn't care about anyone but yourself; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how all of this has been translated, but I cannot remember having said something like that, that I did not care. Because, at any rate, even had I said something like that, heaven forbid, that I did not care, it cannot be said that way, when I took care of food and accommodation and various resources, and now I'm saying that I didn't care. I don't know what was done with this. I don't know how this was translated. I cannot remember that I said something like that. Had I said -- if I said something like that, I apologise, I truly apologise. I said a few minutes ago that I cared, I really cared. Perhaps not the right word was chosen. I did not know what was going on. Perhaps this was not translated quite concretely. It's not that I did not care. Indeed I cared, because these were my friends and colleagues, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'll show you the document, then.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not doubting your document. Please, I'm not doubting your document. I'm just saying that I cannot allow myself to have said something like that. I don't know whether it was translated properly or whether I blurted out something. It is a possibility that I said that I did not know what was going on, but that I said that I did not care what was going on, I could not accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start from the end. I'll start from the end, since you cautioned me, and this is an answer to a question, and the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. question was not read out to us and I'm going to read the question now. In response to Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. The interpreters do not have this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just slow down, Mr. Bakrac. This is not a speed test for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Especially not at the end of a working day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Q. Do you know what punishment was envisaged for stealing bread in your civilian part, for example?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, my goodness. In the civilian part, I don't know what was there, not at all. So ultimately, I'm not interested in what took place in the civilian part or what happened in the military part, where I was not responsible. It seems to me that you really want to accuse me of something that I'm not guilty of. Can you explain this to us? Did you mean, generally speaking, that you did not care about what was going on, or can you explain to us what you were thinking when you made this kind of statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood this, it is a question of bread, and in that case, really, because I did not know what would happen if a convict had stolen a piece of bread or did I see a detainee steal a slice of bread, I could not have known what could have happened or what would have been done about that slice of bread. Because that seems strange to me that for a slice of bread, even in wartime, that somebody would have to be held accountable for that. That's the sense in which I meant it. And this other thing, no way. Heaven forbid. I would never say anything like that, even in the hardest possible situation. I wouldn't have said that for them or for anyone. It just had to do with a slice of bread, and I did not know if something like that was happening, whether somebody punished them for that or not. In my opinion, they should not have been punished. Nobody should be punished for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you quite directly in respect of this. In response to my learned friend's questions, you were telling us about your suffering. Do you think that the Muslim detainees also suffered because they were detained at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I compare this to this time that I have spent now in gaol, since I am suffering, most probably they have suffered too. Because, please, when they gave statements, when listening to their statements, their witness statements, when they made these statements, believe me that I was living through all of this as if I had felt all of that myself. I'm in prison too. So a lot in respect of what will happen to me depends on their statements, and I'm not to be blamed at all for the statements that they have given, for what they have said in their statements, and their statements are not entirely truthful, but their statements can be one of the reasons why I am here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My learned friend read out a sentence to you from the interview that you gave on the 6th of June, 2000, on page 30. If the Prosecution agrees, this is one sentence. I'm going to repeat it so that we do not waste time. I don't want to give it to you to read it. This is in line 28 in the B/C/S version. You said, "One morning the commander of the Tactical Group came. He came to my office. We said hello and he asked me, 'Milorad, could I do a job at your place?'" Can you explain this, what this meant, "at your place"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD KRNOJELAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether he said, "I would like to do a job. I would like to do something in your office, at your place. Three detainees will come, so that I can talk to them." Of course I said that that was all right, and I ordered coffee, but I did not attend the meeting. They just had this coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn in a moment. We're not sitting tomorrow because of the security requirements for the building. We'll resume on Wednesday. Mr. Bakrac, without in any way seeking to limit you, have you got any idea how long you may be on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we still owe you some translations and some documents. As for the re-examination, I don't think it will go on for longer than half an hour, that is to say, technical questions regarding the tendering of certain translations into evidence. As for the Defence, I think that we will be able to finish everything during the first morning session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What we have in mind in relation to the final briefs would be to require them to be delivered, filed, by Friday, the 13th, which would give you more than the week that you were originally promised, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and then list the matter for oral submissions the following Wednesday, the 18th. I want to remind both parties that the written submissions, the final brief, is not intended to be a complete review of the whole trial. We have the transcript. We have very careful summaries of the evidence. What we want to know are the submissions that each party wants to make on the various factual issues which we have to determine, and we don't want it expressed in long, argumentive pages. We want your submission, any brief argument you want to put in support of it, and the transcript references of the evidence you want us to read in relation to that particular matter. If you have any further legal submissions, that is, further to the legal submissions you made in your Pre-Trial briefs, by all means add to them, but we don't want you merely to repeat them. Then, when we come back for the oral arguments, we will, of course, allow you to make some final peroration on behalf of the Prosecution and the Defence, but we would not expect that to be of any substantial length. What we expect you to do mainly in those oral submissions is to provide an answer, where you wish to, to any of the submissions put in the written final briefs. In the final briefs, yes, in the final written briefs. So there is not a lot of repetition. Now, we won't make those orders just at this stage, but we would like to hear from you on Wednesday morning whether you have any reasonable objection to those dates. We are very anxious that we are able to be able to start making some fairly final decisions on factual issues before the end of the month so that the writing of the judgement can be well underway during the summer vacation. So with those admonitions, we'll adjourn now until 9.30 on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 4th day of July, 2001, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.05 p.m.,
